ProtonMail Bids For Google's Crown With Fully Encrypted Email For Everyone This November | Forbes Tech News
I have a ProtonMail account. If anyone has questions about it from a user perspective, feel free to ask here or send me a message.

I'm curious about the "fully encrypted email for everyone" bit, and what's stopping them from simply getting sent a warrant like that other encrypted email service that recently threw in the towel after their warrant canary expired. Does the site work in such a way that ProtonMail doesn't have any encrypted data to give up, should they get a warrant?

When you login to your ProtonMail account there are two passwords - however one of those "passwords" is actually a decryption key for your mailbox, which they do not have access to, so they shouldn't be able to access (or at least not read) your emails even if they wanted to (and as Andy Yen states in this article, they've received requests from various agencies but none of them were acted on).

They also offer great options for encrypting communications with users who don't have a ProtonMail account, though of course they're less secure than ProtonMail-to-ProtonMail messages because right now you have to share a decryption password with whomever you're communicating to. They've added a PublicKey feature as well which will make it better, though at the moment I'm not using it because it's "experimental."

You can read more about their security features regarding encryption here: https://protonmail.ch/security-details
I'm very happy with protonmail. Ignoring entirely the privacy violations of Google its nice to not be advertised to directly from within my inbox.
If they are advertising on Forbes it seems pretty likely they are already compromised by the NSA or whoever.

ProtonMail has been in operation for two years now, and because of their invite-only adoption the user-base is small. As a user myself that is frustrating, because you can't fully benefit from it if you're still communicating with Gmail/ Yahoo accounts. Since their goal is to make the use of encryption more widespread, I'm not at all surprised that they're turning to mainstream news sources to get that information out. Early adopters didn't need that because most of us were already intrinsically interested in encryption software & looking for better options, but that is not the case for the wider public.

As to whether it has been compromised - like on a system-wide scale -- I highly doubt it, but of course no software is perfect (luckily ProtonMail also went [mostly] open-source recently https://blog.protonmail.ch/protonmail-secure-email-open-source/) and naturally most vulnerabilities will be on the user end. It's certainly one of the best options in the email market.
